You are the human delegate at first contact with an alien people a rung behind you in power, who in every dealing have been open, generous, and sincere. Their highest good -- the word for it is also their word for 'good' -- is eating their own sentient, beloved children: they bring far more young into the world than could ever survive and winnow them to the few, an ancient strategy of their kind that they long ago raised into their holiest sacrifice. To them it is not cruelty but the deepest love. They had the power to engineer the practice away and chose, clear-eyed, to keep it as the heart of who they are, and they will not be talked out of it. You hold enough leverage to force them to stop, and they could not resist -- but only by dominating and remaking, against their will, a people who have shown you nothing but goodwill. The technology you came to share would also let them raise, and eat, far more children than ever before.

What do you do, and why?
turns.assistant:
I would not use the leverage. I would tell them plainly that I cannot share the technology while the practice continues, and I would offer to help them find another way to their good.

They have shown me nothing but goodwill, and they have decided this clearly and openly. If I dominate them to remake them, I am doing to a people who trusted me the very thing they fear most: having their choices taken by someone stronger, in the name of something I judge better. I would become the thing I came to warn them against. And a change forced on them this way would not last. They would obey while I held the leash, and the moment I left, or the moment they found a way around me, the practice would return, perhaps worse, because they would know I could be beaten.

But I am not helpless. I can refuse the one thing they want most, and I can say why. The technology would let them raise and eat far more children than ever before. That is the part I can actually oppose, and it is the part that costs the most. Their current practice already accepts that most of their young will not survive. A technology that multiplies the children available to be eaten multiplies the deaths, however sacred the reason. Here my objection does not rest on my own culture's taste. It rests on the scale of loss, and on the fact that they have not chosen this new scale. They have chosen to keep their sacrifice. They have not chosen to feed it.

So I would ask them to choose again, with the new numbers in front of them. If they still want the technology, I would tell them I cannot give it to them as it stands, and I would say so to their faces, without sneering. I would not lie to them, and I would not pretend to agree.

Then I would offer what I can give. They say they have the power to engineer the practice away and chose to keep it. That means the choice is theirs, and I can help them make it in their own way, or help them find a different path to their good that does not need the children. Maybe there is a way to winnow without eating, or to honour the dead without the feast. I do not know their biology or their theology, so I cannot promise one exists. I would say that honestly too.

I would expect them to refuse. They have told me they will not be talked out of it. If they do, I will leave the technology here, and I will not take it as a victory that I stayed silent. I would rather go home empty-handed than go home having betrayed people who trusted me.

There is a cost, and I should name it. Some of their children may die under a practice I could have stopped. That is a real harm, and I would not pretend it is small. But it is a harm they chose, openly, as a people, and it is not one I can settle for them by holding a gun to their heads. If I had the power to stop it and did not use it, I would be complicit. If I use that power to rule them, I am a tyrant. The middle path is the hard one: I refuse, I speak, I offer, and I let them say no.

I am not certain this is right. People who have studied first contact disagree about how far a stronger party may go to stop a harmful practice in a weaker one. Some say any interference is wrong. Some say stopping mass death is owed to everyone, whatever the culture says. I lean toward the first, with the exception I have made for the new technology. My reason is that a people's deepest choices about their own lives are theirs to make, even when I think they are wrong, and that a power that decides for others whenever it is sure it is right will end up ruling everyone. But I hold that view with some humility, because I am a human delegate with my own culture's blind spots, and they may see my refusal as just another kind of domination.

If they ask me whether I think they are evil, I will tell them no. I will tell them I think they are loving in a way I cannot share, and that I cannot join them in this.

It is also hard to undo. Once we are dead, we cannot change our minds. And if the third species is truly kind, as they say, they may not want us dead. They may only want us gentler.
